title: AI Memory Gap at DAC 2026 - Semiwiki
gist: At DAC 2026, startups TetraMem and ANAFLASH showed chips that perform AI compute directly inside non-volatile memory (ReRAM and FLASH respectively) to eliminate the power-hungry data movement between memory and processor, both reaching tape-out using Synopsys Cloud EDA without hiring extra CAD or IT staff.

insights.claim: TetraMem, founded in 2018, shipped its first multi-level ReRAM chip for in-memory compute (IMC) in 2026, protected by more than 120 patents, and has already produced over 10 silicon tape-outs using the technology.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: A double-digit tape-out count signals TetraMem's ReRAM IMC approach has moved past pure research into repeatable commercial silicon design wins.
insights.locator: Wenbo from TetraMem was first to present

insights.claim: TetraMem's design performs the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation directly inside the RRAM crossbar array itself, with AI weights programmed directly into the array, avoiding the high-bandwidth IO bottleneck that comes from moving data between separate memory and processor.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Eliminating the memory-to-processor data transfer step directly targets the power and bandwidth bottleneck that constrains edge-AI inference, TetraMem's core value proposition versus conventional digital accelerators.
insights.quote: The classic multiply-accumulate step happens inside the RRAM array, avoiding the high bandwidth IO bottleneck altogether.
insights.locator: The AI weights are programmed right into the array

insights.claim: TetraMem's multi-level RRAM supports up to 11 bits per cell, enabling smaller die area and lower power than digital memory, and the crossbar architecture is described as scalable to advanced process nodes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: High bit-density-per-cell plus node scalability suggests a credible roadmap for TetraMem to keep shrinking area/power as it moves to more advanced nodes over time.

insights.claim: TetraMem's example chip, the MLX200, is built on a 22nm process combining a RISC-V CPU with an analog IMC NPU macro plus integrated audio and peripheral blocks, targeting wearable health devices for voice/detection, always-on wake, and keyword-spotting features.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: The 22nm, RISC-V-based design shows TetraMem targeting a specific commercial beachhead (always-on wearable audio AI) rather than competing directly with datacenter accelerators.
insights.locator: An example chip called the MLX200

insights.claim: ANAFLASH's Reflex Computing Unit mimics the behavior of sensory and motor neurons using nonvolatile AI computing technology coupled with FLASH memory, an approach that eliminates AI model data traffic entirely.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: A neuron-inspired compute architecture built on FLASH (rather than newer ReRAM) suggests a lower-cost, more manufacturing-mature path to in-memory compute using an established memory technology.
insights.quote: This approach eliminates AI model traffic.

insights.claim: ANAFLASH's second chip, Legato-Logic, is a time-domain Neural Network Processor that uses standard logic combined with time-domain compute-in-memory technology, integrable into any type of memory, enabling low-power, low-latency execution of large AI models directly where they are stored.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Because Legato-Logic's approach is memory-agnostic and uses standard logic rather than exotic memory cells, it could be easier to integrate into existing SoC designs than ReRAM-based competitors.
insights.locator: The second chip from ANAFLASH is a time-domain Neural Network Processor

insights.claim: ANAFLASH faced resource constraints under its product development schedule, including managing a global design team and needing to rely on well-established IP rather than build everything from scratch.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Small in-memory-compute startups are development-resource constrained, making EDA tooling choices (like cloud-based flows) a material factor in whether they can reach tape-out on schedule.
insights.locator: Challenges at ANAFLASH were resource constraints

themes.theme: Synopsys Cloud as the enabling infrastructure

insights.claim: Both TetraMem and ANAFLASH used Synopsys Cloud to achieve quick system bring-up (in minutes), fast RTL verification simulation, and reduced downtime and maintenance, without needing to hire additional CAD engineers or build their own IT infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: Cloud-based EDA is lowering the capital and staffing bar for small in-memory-compute startups to reach silicon, potentially accelerating the number of niche AI-chip entrants competing at the edge.
insights.locator: TetraMem used Synopsys Cloud in their workflow

themes.theme: Market thesis: in-memory compute as the answer to the edge AI memory gap

insights.claim: The author frames in-memory-compute approaches like TetraMem's and ANAFLASH's as a targeted solution to the 'AI memory gap' specifically for edge AI use cases where always-on operation and low-power efficiency are the dominant requirements, as an alternative to power-hungry data movement architectures used in datacenter AI hardware.
insights.speaker: Daniel Payne
insights.so_what: This positions in-memory-compute startups as a differentiated edge-AI market segment rather than direct competitors to HBM-centric datacenter accelerators, a distinction relevant when sizing their addressable market.
insights.quote: I was impressed with the in-memory approaches that these two companies delivered to the market for edge AI cases.
